chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
In rental real estate, profitability isn't guessed: it's calculated. Three simple indicators — cash flow, the capitalization rate (cap rate), and the gross rent multiplier (GRM) — tell you in a few minutes whether a building is worth an offer.

This guide explains each calculation, with clear examples, so you can compare buildings objectively.

Each chapter ends with a lined « My notes » page for you to work out YOUR own numbers.

chapters.title: Net operating income (NOI)
chapters.objective: Calculate what the building generates before financing.
chapters.html:
Calculate what the building generates before financing.

Net operating income (NOI) is the basis for everything: rental income (minus vacancy) less operating expenses (taxes, insurance, maintenance, management, common-area energy) — BUT before mortgage payments.

Example: rents of $36,000/year − 5% vacancy ($1,800) = $34,200; expenses $12,000; NOI = $22,200.

Emilie's tip

Never confuse gross rents with NOI. A building with high rents but high expenses can generate less NOI than a more modest, efficient one.

chapters.title: Cash flow
chapters.objective: Know what actually stays in your pocket.
chapters.html:
Know what actually stays in your pocket.

Cash flow is NOI minus mortgage payments (principal + interest). It is the money left each year after paying for EVERYTHING. Positive cash flow is generally the goal; negative cash flow means you are funding the building out of your own pocket.

Example: NOI $22,200 − mortgage $18,000/year = cash flow of $4,200/year.

Emilie's tip

Slightly positive or neutral cash flow can be acceptable if the building is appreciating and the tenant is paying down your principal. But large negative cash flow is a risk, especially if rates rise.

chapters.title: The capitalization rate (cap rate)
chapters.html:
Compare buildings independently of financing.

The capitalization rate = NOI ÷ purchase price, expressed as a percentage. It measures the building's return before financing, which lets you compare buildings against one another and against their area.

Example: NOI $22,200 ÷ price $400,000 = a 5.55% cap rate. A higher cap rate means (all else being equal) a better return — but sometimes more risk or a less desirable area.

Emilie's tip

Always compare a building's cap rate to those in the same area. An abnormally high cap rate often hides something: a poor neighbourhood, major work ahead, or unsustainable rents.

chapters.title: The GRM and the limits of ratios
chapters.objective: Use a quick benchmark and know its limits.
chapters.html:
Use a quick benchmark and know its limits.

The gross rent multiplier (GRM) = purchase price ÷ annual gross income. It is a QUICK comparison benchmark (a lower GRM is generally more attractive), but a crude one because it ignores expenses.

  • GRM: good for a quick first screen, not for deciding.
  • Cap rate and cash flow: more reliable because they account for expenses (and financing, for cash flow).
  • Always validate with the real numbers before making an offer.
Emilie's tip

Use the GRM for an initial screen, never for a final decision. Two buildings with the same GRM can be very different once the real expenses are factored in.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Gather the real rents and expenses of the target building.
  2. Calculate the NOI.

Within 30 days

  1. Calculate cash flow, cap rate, and GRM.
  2. Compare against other buildings and the area's cap rate.

Then

  1. Decide whether to offer based on validated numbers, with Emilie.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• NOI: net operating income, income minus expenses, before financing.
  • Cash flow: NOI minus mortgage payments.
  • Cap rate: NOI ÷ purchase price, the return before financing.
  • GRM: price ÷ gross income, a quick comparison benchmark.
  • Vacancy: the percentage of lost rent to build into the calculations.
